mainTopic: Correcting omissions in the עמידה, the meaning of קבע, short prayers in danger, and תפלת הדרך
overview: The גמרא first finishes a point about someone who remembers a missed request only after שומע תפילה. It then teaches where a person returns if he forgot the ראש חודש addition in the עמידה. רב פפא and רב נחמן בר יצחק refine this rule: moving one's feet matters, and so does whether the person regularly says תחנונים after praying. Next the גמרא explains רבי אליעזר's warning against prayer that is קבע. It offers several meanings, including prayer that feels like a burden, prayer without pleading, prayer with nothing new, and missing the time of דמדומי חמה. It then explains the phrase פרשת העבור and lists several short prayers for dangerous places, and רב הונא rules like אחרים. Finally, אליהו's advice to 'consult your Creator' is identified as תפלת הדרך, which every traveler must say, and its full text is given. אביי begins a new statement at the very end, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Remembering only after the prayer-request blessing
steps.stepSummary: The previous ruling applies when the person remembers after שומע תפילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: That case is when the person remembered after שומע תפילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows an earlier ruling. This line completes the previous discussion before moving to a new case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שומע תפילה was still a place to add the missed request. Once the person has passed it, that option is gone.

phrases.english: That is when he remembered after ‘Who hears prayer.’

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an exchange that began on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the earlier ruling to a particular point in the prayer.
steps.terutzMaskana: The earlier ruling concerns remembering after שומע תפילה.

steps.title: Where to return after omitting the New Moon addition
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי gives return points for someone who omitted the ראש חודש addition.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי תנחום said in the name of רב אסי, who said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: If someone omitted the New Moon addition in the service blessing, he returns to that blessing. The same applies if he remembers during thanksgiving or the peace blessing. If he finished, he returns to the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a new ruling about a missed ראש חודש addition. It lists where the person returns, depending on when he remembers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Remembering in either later blessing sends him back to עבודה, where the addition belongs. The initial ruling says that finishing the עמידה sends him back to the beginning; the next step will clarify what counts as finishing.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם אָמַר רַב אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Tanchum said that Rav Asi said that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:

phrases.aramaic: טָעָה וְלֹא הִזְכִּיר שֶׁל רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ בָּ״עֲבוֹדָה״ — חוֹזֵר לָ״עֲבוֹדָה״.
phrases.english: If he erred and did not mention the New Moon in the service blessing, he returns to the service blessing.
If he remembered in the thanksgiving blessing, he returns to the service blessing.
If he remembered in ‘Grant peace,’ he returns to the service blessing.
And if he finished, he returns to the beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם אָמַר רַב אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a separate case after the earlier discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After omitting the ראש חודש addition, return to עבודה if still in the later blessings; if the prayer is finished, return to its beginning.

steps.title: What counts as having finished
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בריה דרב אחא בר אדא limits the instruction to start over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא בריה דרב אחא בר אדא said: The rule that someone who finished must return to the beginning applies only if he moved his feet. If he did not move his feet, he returns to the service blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא clarifies the word “finished” from the previous ruling. It sets up two different outcomes based on whether the person moved his feet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Merely reaching the end does not yet require starting the whole עמידה again. If he has not moved his feet, he can still return to עבודה.

keyTerms.meaning: moved his feet from his place

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא:
phrases.english: Rav Pappa, son of Rav Acha bar Adda, said:
What we said—that if he finished, he returns to the beginning—
we said only when he had moved his feet.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא עָקַר רַגְלָיו — חוֹזֵר לָעֲבוֹדָה.
phrases.english: But if he had not moved his feet, he returns to the service blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַחָא בַּר אַדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Qualifies the previous step’s rule for someone who finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Returning to the beginning requires having moved one’s feet; otherwise, return to עבודה.

steps.title: Asking for the source of the distinction
steps.stepSummary: Someone asks where the distinction about moving one’s feet came from.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Where do you have this from?
steps.whatsHappening: A questioner asks for the source of the clarification just given. The question is about its authority, not about what its words mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The preceding step added a condition to the rule about finishing. The questioner now asks how the speaker knows that condition.

keyTerms.meaning: where do you get it from

phrases.english: He said to him: Where do you get this from?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Requests support for the distinction stated in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the rule that moving one’s feet changes where the person must return.

steps.title: Tracing the ruling back to רב
steps.stepSummary: The speaker says he heard the ruling from his father, who heard it from רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I heard it from my father and teacher, and my father and teacher heard it from רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The speaker answers by giving the chain through which he received the ruling. This closes the exchange about its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not add another case or change the rule. It identifies who transmitted the distinction stated in step 3.
steps.whatToRemember: For the missed ראש חודש addition, רב פפא's distinction is whether the person moved his feet: if not, he returns to עבודה; if he did, he starts the עמידה again. רב נחמן בר יצחק qualifies this in the next two steps.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מֵאַבָּא מָרִי שְׁמִיעַ לִי,
phrases.english: He said to him: I heard it from my father and teacher,
and my father and teacher heard it from Rav.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מֵאַבָּא מָרִי שְׁמִיעַ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for the ruling’s source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He received the ruling from his father, who received it from רב.

steps.title: Regular supplications can keep the prayer open
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק limits the rule that moving one’s feet requires starting over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק says: The rule that someone who moved his feet returns to the beginning applies when he does not regularly say supplications after his prayer. If he regularly says them, he returns to the blessing of עבודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a qualification to the earlier rule. Moving one’s feet does not require starting over if the person regularly says תחנונים afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier rule treated moving one’s feet as the point after which a return must begin at the start. רב נחמן בר יצחק says that regular תחנונים afterward change the return point to עבודה.

keyTerms.meaning: moved his feet at the end of prayer
to the blessing of Temple service

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא דַּאֲמַרַן עָקַר רַגְלָיו חוֹזֵר לָרֹאשׁ
phrases.english: What we said—that if he moved his feet, he returns to the beginning—
we said only when he is not accustomed
to saying supplications after his prayer.
But if he is accustomed to saying supplications
after his prayer, he returns to the blessing of Temple service.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: הָא דַּאֲמַרַן עָקַר רַגְלָיו חוֹזֵר לָרֹאשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It adds a qualification to the return-point ruling whose source was just identified.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone accustomed to saying תחנונים after prayer returns to עבודה even after moving his feet.

steps.title: A second version limits the shorter return
steps.stepSummary: An alternate version of רב נחמן בר יצחק limits the rule for someone who has not moved his feet.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב נחמן בר יצחק taught this instead: Returning to עבודה before moving one’s feet applies when the person regularly says תחנונים after prayer. Without that regular practice, he returns to the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of the same teaching. This version qualifies the rule for someone who has not moved his feet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, regular תחנונים create an exception after the person moved his feet. Here, regular תחנונים are required for the shorter return even before he moves them.

keyTerms.meaning: he has not moved his feet

steps.confusionAlert: These are two versions of where the qualification applies, not two consecutive instructions for the same case.

phrases.aramaic: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Some say that Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:

phrases.aramaic: הָא דַּאֲמַרַן כִּי לֹא עָקַר רַגְלָיו
phrases.english: What we said—that when he has not moved his feet,
he returns to the blessing of Temple service—we said
only when he is accustomed to saying supplications

phrases.aramaic: אַחַר תְּפִלָּתוֹ, אֲבָל אִם אֵינוֹ רָגִיל
phrases.english: after his prayer. But if he is not accustomed
to saying supplications after his prayer,
he returns to the beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It gives an alternate wording of the qualification in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, someone who has not moved his feet returns to עבודה only if he regularly says תחנונים afterward.

steps.title: What does fixed prayer mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי אליעזר and asks what he means by קֶבַע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says, ‘Anyone who makes his prayer fixed,’ and so on. What does ‘fixed’ mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to רבי אליעזר’s statement and sets up a new discussion. It asks what קֶבַע means here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quoted statement gives the word being examined. The question asks for its meaning; the next teachings will offer answers.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage whose statement is being explained
fixed or set; the word under discussion
and so on; marks an abbreviated quotation

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר כׇּל הָעוֹשֶׂה תְּפִלָּתוֹ קֶבַע וְכוּ׳:
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: Anyone who makes his prayer fixed, and so on.
What does “fixed” mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion leaves the return-point rules and opens a question about רבי אליעזר’s wording.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The intended meaning of קֶבַע in רבי אליעזר’s statement.

steps.title: Prayer feels like a burden
steps.stepSummary: רבי אושעיא explains קֶבַע as prayer that feels like a burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אידי reports רבי אושעיא’s answer: It refers to anyone whose prayer feels like a burden to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first answer to its question about קֶבַע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer looks at the person’s experience while praying. Prayer is קֶבַע in this sense when it feels like something heavy to get through.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage to whom the explanation is attributed

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ya’akov bar Idi said that Rabbi Oshaya said:
Anyone whose prayer seems to him like a burden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It supplies the first meaning of the word asked about in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קֶבַע describes prayer that feels like a burden to the person.

steps.title: Prayer is not spoken as a plea
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים explain קֶבַע through the way the prayer is spoken.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן say: It refers to anyone who does not say the prayer in language of supplication.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another answer to the question about קֶבַע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous answer focused on how prayer feels to the person. This answer focuses on how the person says it: not as a plea.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ אוֹמְרָהּ בִּלְשׁוֹן תַּחֲנוּנִים.
phrases.english: Anyone who does not say it in language of supplication.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It offers another explanation of קֶבַע alongside step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קֶבַע describes prayer not spoken in a pleading manner.

steps.title: Prayer has no new element
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף offer a third explanation of קֶבַע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both say: It refers to anyone who cannot introduce something new into the prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer to the question about קֶבַע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer focuses on whether the person can add something new to the prayer. The next speaker will respond to this particular explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: the two sages giving this explanation
to introduce something new into it

phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef both said:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְחַדֵּשׁ בָּהּ דָּבָר.
phrases.english: Anyone who cannot introduce something new into it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It adds a third explanation of קֶבַע, after the explanation about speaking in supplication.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קֶבַע describes prayer in which the person cannot introduce anything new.

steps.title: Adding something new can be distracting
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא says he could add something new but fears becoming distracted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: I can introduce something new into the prayer, but I am afraid I might become distracted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא responds to the idea of adding something new to prayer. He says he can do it, but worries it will disrupt his concentration.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His concern shows a practical difficulty with adding something new. He does not say that he lacks the ability; he says he fears what may happen when he uses it.

keyTerms.meaning: the sage describing his own practice

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא distinguishes being able to add something new from choosing to do so when it may distract him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
I can introduce something new into it,
but I am afraid that perhaps I will become distracted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: אֲנָא יָכֵילְנָא לְחַדּוֹשֵׁי בַּהּ מִילְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It responds specifically to the explanation in step 11 about introducing something new.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי זירא can add something new to prayer but avoids doing so out of concern that he will become distracted.

steps.title: A fourth way to understand fixed prayer
steps.stepSummary: אביי בר אבין and רבי חנינא בר אבין say that someone who does not pray when the sun is reddening makes prayer קֶבַע.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי בר אבין and רבי חנינא בר אבין both say: It refers to anyone who does not pray when the sun is reddening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another answer to the earlier question about קֶבַע. This answer focuses on when a person prays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier answers focused on a person’s attitude or manner of speaking. This answer points instead to missing a valued time for prayer.

keyTerms.meaning: one of the two sages giving this explanation

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּיֵי בַּר אָבִין וְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אָבִין
phrases.english: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Ḥanina bar Avin
who both said:
Anyone who does not pray
when the sun is reddening.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי בַּר אָבִין וְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אָבִין דְאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another explanation after רבי זירא’s comment.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: קֶבַע can describe someone who does not pray at דמדומי חמה.

steps.title: A teaching supports this prayer time
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן calls prayer at דמדומי חמה a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: It is a מצוה to pray when the sun is reddening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the new explanation with a teaching about the value of this prayer time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This teaching explains why missing that time could matter. It does not yet address a possible risk in waiting until sunset.

keyTerms.meaning: for he said; introduces supporting teaching
the sage whose teaching is quoted

phrases.english: For Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said
in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
It is a מצוה to pray
when the sun is reddening.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies support for the importance of the time named in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: The value of praying at דמדומי חמה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The teaching of רבי יוחנן, reported by רבי חייא בר אבא.

steps.title: A verse is offered for the timing
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא quotes a verse linking reverence for God with the sun and moon.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי זירא said: What is the verse? “May they fear You with the sun and before the moon, generation after generation.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a verse connected to prayer near the sun’s transitions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse speaks of fearing God “with the sun” and “before the moon.” רבי זירא uses those words to support the special timing just discussed.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Zeira said: What is the verse?
“May they fear You with the sun
and before the moon, generation after generation.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a verse after the teaching that praises this prayer time.
steps.raayaObject: The special value of prayer timed near the sun.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ״יִירָאוּךָ עִם שָׁמֶשׁ וְלִפְנֵי יָרֵחַ דּוֹר דּוֹרִים״.

steps.title: A practice raises a concern about sunset
steps.stepSummary: In the West, people strongly objected to praying at דמדומי חמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the West, they cursed someone who prayed when the sun was reddening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now reports a practice that seems to conflict with the praise of this prayer time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous teachings call this timing valuable. The reported objection creates a question: why would anyone discourage it?

keyTerms.meaning: in the West, meaning the Land of Israel here

phrases.english: In the West, they cursed
someone who prayed
when the sun was reddening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a contrary practice after the teaching and verse in favor of this timing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The praise of praying at דמדומי חמה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A practice that strongly discourages this timing appears hard to square with calling it a מצוה.

steps.title: The concern is missing the time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that a delay might cause someone to lose the chance to pray on time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Perhaps the hour will get away from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why that practice objected and immediately gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Waiting for the right moment near sunset has a risk: a person might lose track of the time. The objection addresses that practical danger, even though the timing itself was praised.

keyTerms.meaning: the hour may get away from him

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Perhaps the hour will get away from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא — דִּלְמָא מִיטַּרְפָא לֵיהּ שַׁעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the concern behind the opposing practice.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person waiting until near sunset might miss the time for prayer.
steps.whatToRemember: The special timing is praised, but waiting for it can create a practical risk.

steps.title: What does the phrase in the short prayer mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to רבי יהושע’s short prayer and asks about פָּרָשַׁת הָעִבּוּר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says that someone walking in a dangerous place recites a short prayer, and so on, including “at every פרשת העבור.” What does “פרשת העבור” mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the relevant part of רבי יהושע’s teaching and sets up a question about its wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not whether to say a short prayer in danger. It asks what one unusual phrase within that prayer means.

keyTerms.meaning: the phrase whose meaning is being examined

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says: Someone who is walking
in a dangerous place recites a short prayer
and so on: “at every parashat ha’ibur.”
What does “parashat ha’ibur” mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of prayer timing and turns to wording in the short prayer.

steps.title: Needs are remembered even during anger
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא reports מר עוקבא’s reading: even when God is angry with Israel, their needs should remain before Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא: Even when You are filled with anger toward them like a pregnant woman, may all their needs be before You.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one explanation of the difficult phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reading connects הָעִבּוּר with both anger and pregnancy. The prayer asks that anger not cause the people’s needs to be overlooked.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said in the name of Mar Ukva:
Even at a time when You are filled
with anger toward them, like a pregnant woman—
may all their needs be before You.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about פָּרָשַׁת הָעִבּוּר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase asks for compassion even when God is filled with anger.

steps.title: Needs are remembered even after wrongdoing
steps.stepSummary: A second version of מר עוקבא’s explanation refers to people violating words of תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב חסדא said in the name of מר עוקבא: Even when they violate the words of the תורה, may all their needs be before You.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of the answer to the same wording question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version connects הָעִבּוּר with עוֹבְרִים, “violating.” The request stays the same: may their needs remain before God even when they have done wrong.

phrases.english: Some say

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said in the name of Mar Ukva:
Even when they violate
the words of the Torah—
may all their needs be before You.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר מָר עוּקְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the same phrase.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase asks for compassion even when the people violate דברי תורה.
steps.whatToRemember: Both readings ask that people’s needs be heard in a difficult moment; they differ about what הָעִבּוּר points to.

steps.title: Which short prayer is said in danger?
steps.stepSummary: A teaching describes travel among wild animals and robbers, then asks for the wording of the short prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: Someone walking where there are bands of wild animals and robbers recites a short prayer. And what is the short prayer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces another teaching about prayer in danger and sets up the different wordings that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dangerous setting explains why the prayer is shortened. The question now seeks the words to say, not an explanation of פָּרָשַׁת הָעִבּוּר.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: Someone walking
in a place with bands of wild animals and robbers
recites a short prayer,
and what is the short prayer?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַמְהַלֵּךְ בִּמְקוֹם גְּדוּדֵי חַיָּה וְלִסְטִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining one prayer’s wording to presenting additional short-prayer formulas.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The wording of a short prayer said in this dangerous setting.

steps.title: One wording asks God to do what is good
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר gives a short prayer asking for God’s will, reassurance for those who fear Him, and what is good in His eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: “Do Your will in the heavens above; give peace of mind to those who fear You below; and do what is good in Your eyes. Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי אליעזר’s answer to the question of what to say.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His wording makes broad requests rather than listing specific needs. It ends with a blessing about God hearing prayer.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
“Do Your will in the heavens above,
and give peace of mind to those who fear You below,
and do what is good in Your eyes.
Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the first wording requested in step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר’s formula for the short prayer.

steps.title: Another wording asks for Israel’s request
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע gives a different short prayer asking God to hear Israel’s cry and respond quickly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says: “Hear the cry of Your people Israel, and quickly fulfill their request. Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יהושע’s alternative wording for the short prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version directly asks God to hear the people and answer them quickly. Like the previous version, it ends with the blessing about God hearing prayer.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says:
“Hear the cry of Your people Israel,
and quickly fulfill their request.
Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second wording alongside רבי אליעזר’s formula.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהושע’s formula for the short prayer.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק gives another short prayer
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק asks God to hear Israel and quickly grant their request.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק says: “Hear the outcry of Your people, Israel, and quickly fulfill their request. Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”
steps.whatsHappening: The earlier question asked for the wording of a short prayer. רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק now supplies another version.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version is almost identical to רבי יהושע's. The only difference is צַעֲקַת ('outcry') in place of שַׁוְעַת ('cry'). Like the others, it ends with the blessing for hearing prayer.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, says:
“Hear the outcry of Your people, Israel,
and quickly fulfill their request,
blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third answer to the question about the short prayer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A prayer asking God to hear Israel's cry and promptly grant their request.

steps.title: אחרים give a prayer for needs people cannot fully express
steps.stepSummary: אחרים ask God to provide for each person’s needs, even when people cannot state all those needs themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחרים say: “The needs of Your people, Israel, are many, and their understanding is limited. May it be Your will, Lord our God, to give each person enough for sustenance and each body what it lacks. Blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”
steps.whatsHappening: אחרים give one more wording for the short prayer. This version asks God to meet needs that the person praying may not know how to describe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prayer first says that people have many needs but limited understanding. It then asks God to provide what each person and body actually lacks.

phrases.english: Others say:
“The needs of Your people, Israel, are many
and their understanding is limited.
May it be Your will, Lord our God,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁתִּתֵּן לְכׇל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד כְּדֵי פַרְנָסָתוֹ,
phrases.english: that You give each and every person enough for his sustenance,
and each and every body enough to meet what it lacks,
blessed are You, Lord, Who hears prayer.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers another answer to the same question, with a different focus.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A prayer asking God to supply each person's sustenance and bodily needs.

steps.title: רב הונא selects the wording of אחרים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that the הלכה follows אחרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: The הלכה follows אחרים.
steps.whatsHappening: After the different wordings have been presented, רב הונא says which one to use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a ruling, not another prayer text. It selects the wording of אחרים from the versions just given.

keyTerms.meaning: רב הונא, who gives the ruling

steps.whatToRemember: For this short prayer, רב הונא rules like אחרים.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The ruling follows Others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Chooses the wording proposed in the preceding step.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows the short prayer stated by אחרים.

steps.title: אליהו advises how to act before a journey
steps.stepSummary: אליהו tells רב יהודה to avoid anger and drunkenness, and to consult his Creator before setting out.
steps.simpleTranslation: אליהו said to רב יהודה, the brother of רב סלא חסידא: “Do not become angry and do not sin. Do not become drunk and do not sin. When you set out on a journey, consult your Creator and then go.”
steps.whatsHappening: The discussion moves from a prayer for danger to advice connected with travel. אליהו gives three instructions, ending with what to do before leaving.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two instructions warn against behavior that can lead to sin. The last instruction introduces an unexplained phrase—“consult your Creator”—which the next step will ask about.

phrases.english: Elijah said to Rav Yehuda,
the brother of Rav Sala the Pious:
Do not become angry, and do not sin.
Do not become drunk, and do not sin.
And when you set out on a journey,
consult your Creator and go.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אֵלִיָּהוּ לְרַב יְהוּדָה אֲחוּהּ דְּרַב סַלָּא חֲסִידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related discussion about what a traveler should do before departure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אליהו advises avoiding anger and drunkenness and consulting one's Creator before travel.

steps.title: What does consulting your Creator mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what action אליהו meant by “consult your Creator and go.”
steps.simpleTranslation: What does “consult your Creator and go” mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses over אליהו’s travel advice and asks what the phrase means in practice. This question sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice says to do something before leaving, but has not named the action. The question asks for that missing detail.

phrases.english: What does “consult your Creator and go” mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical meaning of the final instruction in אליהו’s advice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the traveler should actually do to “consult your Creator.”

steps.title: Consulting your Creator means saying the traveler’s prayer
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב reports רב חסדא’s explanation: the instruction refers to תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב said in the name of רב חסדא: This is the traveler’s prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יעקב, citing רב חסדא, answers the question. The traveler consults God by saying תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer turns אליהו’s general-sounding advice into a named prayer. The next statement will say whether a traveler is required to say it.

keyTerms.meaning: רב חסדא, whose explanation is reported

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rav Hisda:
This is the traveler's prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the action requested by the preceding question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: “Consult your Creator” refers to saying תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ.

steps.title: A traveler must say the traveler’s prayer
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב also reports רב חסדא’s rule that anyone setting out on a journey must say תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יעקב said in the name of רב חסדא: Anyone who sets out on a journey must recite the traveler’s prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יעקב gives a second statement from רב חסדא. It says that saying תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ is required for someone setting out on a journey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step identified the prayer meant by אליהו’s advice. This step adds the rule about who must say it: anyone setting out on a journey.
steps.whatToRemember: אליהו’s “consult your Creator” refers to תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ; רב חסדא says a traveler must recite it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yaakov said in the name of Rav Hisda:
Anyone who sets out on a journey must
recite the traveler's prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an obligation after identifying the prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone setting out on a journey must recite תְּפִלַּת הַדֶּרֶךְ.

steps.title: What is the traveler's prayer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the actual wording of תפלת הדרך.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the traveler's prayer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what words make up the traveler's prayer that רב חסדא just required. This question sets up the next step, where the full text is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא told us we must say תפלת הדרך, but he never told us what to say. A rule is hard to keep if you do not know the words, so the גמרא now asks for the exact text.

keyTerms.meaning: The traveler's prayer, said when setting out on a journey

phrases.english: What is the traveler's prayer?
phrases.notes: This asks for the wording, not whether the prayer is required. That was already settled in Step 30.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the content of the prayer that רב חסדא required in Step 30.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact text of תפלת הדרך.

steps.title: The full text of the traveler's prayer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the wording of תפלת הדרך. It is a request for a safe journey that ends with the ברכה 'שומע תפלה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: May it be Your will, ה׳ my God, that You lead me to peace, direct my steps to peace, and support me to peace. Save me from every enemy and ambush on the way. Send blessing to the work of my hands. Let me find grace, kindness, and mercy in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see me. Blessed are You, ה׳, Who hears prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting the full traveler's prayer, word for word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prayer asks for three main things. First, a peaceful journey (going, walking, and being supported in peace). Second, protection from enemies and ambushers. Third, success and finding favor with ה׳ and with people. It closes with a ברכה, 'שומע תפלה', the same ending used in the weekday שמונה עשרה.

keyTerms.meaning: May it be Your will (a common opening for a personal request)
An enemy and an ambusher (someone lying in wait)

steps.confusionAlert: Notice that the prayer here is written in the singular: 'lead me' and 'my God.' The version in today's סידור is in the plural ('lead us'). The reason for that change is connected to אביי's statement, which begins right after this.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source text for the תפלת הדרך said by travelers today.

phrases.english: May it be Your will, ה׳ my God,
that You lead me to peace,
and direct my steps to peace,
and support me to peace,
and rescue me from the hand of every enemy
and ambusher along the way,
and send blessing to the work of my hands,
and grant me grace, kindness, and mercy
in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see me.
Blessed are You, ה׳, Who hears prayer.
phrases.notes: The prayer ends with a ברכה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The full text of תפלת הדרך, ending with 'ברוך אתה ה׳ שומע תפלה'.

steps.title: אביי begins a new statement: 'Always'
steps.stepSummary: אביי opens a new statement with the word 'לעולם' (always). The rest of his statement continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Always...
steps.whatsHappening: אביי starts a new teaching about this prayer, but only his opening words appear on this amud. This step sets up his full statement, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'לעולם' signals that a general, always-applicable rule is coming. אביי's comment relates to how the traveler's prayer should be said. The full point will become clear when the statement is completed.

keyTerms.meaning: אביי, a leading אמורא in Babylonia
Always / at all times (introduces a general rule)

phrases.english: Abaye said: At all times
phrases.notes: The statement is cut off here and continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the text of the prayer is given, אביי begins a new rule about it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not yet stated. Only the opening word 'לעולם' appears on this amud; the rest of אביי's statement continues on the next amud.
